screens.title: Error Handling in Functions
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we map two common ways functions communicate failure: returning error codes and raising exceptions. You will understand their trade-offs, see concrete Python examples, and learn a practical rule: use exceptions for truly exceptional conditions and use sentinel returns or explicit result values for expected, recoverable outcomes. We'll ground theory with a small divide function and a file-processing exercise so you can practice raising and catching specific errors. As we progress, you’ll spot three common mistakes: using exceptions for normal control flow, swallowing exceptions without logging, and catching broad exception classes that hide problems. Each of these mistakes undermines reliability and slows debugging. By the end, you’ll be able to decide which approach fits a given A P I and how to structure try-except blocks that convey useful context. Think of error codes like traffic lights at many intersections — predictable and local — and exceptions like an ambulance that changes global flow when something truly wrong happens. Consider the functions you write: do callers expect failure as a normal outcome, or is failure surprising? That question will guide everything you see next.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Error Handling Overview
Error Handling in Functions
Compare patterns, decide when to raise, and learn safe exception practices.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Live coding examples, compare error codes with exceptions, and practical refactor patterns to write safer, clearer functions.
In this lesson
We’ll demonstrate both approaches with the same small problems: dividing numbers and reading files. You’ll see the error-code version with explicit status values, then a refactor to specific exceptions and try-except blocks that improve clarity and propagation. The visible code panels are canonical Python examples you can adapt.
# Error code style (compact)
def divide_numbers_with_code(numerator, denominator):
  if denominator == 0:
    return -1, "Error: Cannot divide by zero."
  if not isinstance(numerator, (int, float)) or not isinstance(denominator, (int, float)):
    return -2, "Error: Invalid input types."
  return 0, numerator / denominator

# Exception style (preferred for exceptional cases)
def divide_numbers_with_exception(numerator, denominator):
  if not isinstance(numerator, (int, float)) or not isinstance(denominator, (int, float)):
    raise TypeError("Invalid input types. Both numerator and denominator must be numbers.")
  if denominator == 0:
    raise ValueError("Cannot divide by zero.")
  return numerator / denominator
Traffic-light: error codes
Ambulance: exceptions
Estimated time: 11 minutes mixed media
Quick topics
  • When to return a sentinel value or None
  • When to raise and catch specific exceptions
  • Common mistakes and safe patterns
Explore Key Topics
Compare error codes vs exceptions, practice try-except blocks, and implement a robust file-processing function that raises a clear custom error on bad data.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide practice and assessment. First, you will compare and contrast error codes and exceptions: that means not just naming them, but explaining how they change control flow, caller responsibilities, and debuggability. Second, you will decide when to use exceptions for truly exceptional conditions and when to return sentinel values for expected, recoverable outcomes; this helps you design clean APIs that communicate intent. Third, you will implement robust exception handling in Python using try-except blocks and specific exception types, including raising informative, contextual exceptions. Fourth, you will discuss common mistakes — such as using exceptions for routine control flow, catching overly broad exception classes, or swallowing errors — and apply best practices like logging, re-raising, and choosing the right abstraction level for handlers. Each objective includes a small practice milestone so you can verify competence: explain trade-offs, refactor a function, write a file-processing routine that raises a custom error, and critique a legacy try-except that hides issues. These are skills you’ll want to apply in code reviews and production systems to reduce bugs and improve clarity.

screens.title: What are Error Codes?
screens.narratorSegment: Error codes are explicit return values reserved to communicate success or specific failure types from a function. Historically they appear as integers or tuples where one part is a status and the other is the result or message. The defining characteristic is that the caller must inspect the returned status to detect failures. A straightforward advantage is predictability: when failure is common or expected, returning a sentinel value keeps control local and avoids unwinding the call stack. For example, a parse function may return None or a pair (value, success_flag) when parsing user input is routine and failing is not surprising. But that safety comes at a cost. Requiring the caller to always check the status clutters code and is easy to forget, producing silent failures. Error codes also tend to carry limited diagnostic context compared to exceptions. In practice, clean APIs use sentinel returns for expected, recoverable conditions — for instance, a lookup that might legitimately return no result — and reserve error codes with clear documentation, consistent values, and helper functions to unpack them. A common misconception is thinking error codes are inherently safer; they are explicit but place the burden on every caller. The takeaway: use error codes intentionally for normal, anticipated failures and structure callers to check and handle the codes.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Error codes are explicit status returns used for predictable, expected failures; they require systematic checking by callers.

content.html:
Definition
Core concept
Error Codes explained
A function returns a status value that the caller inspects. Use this when failure is expected and can be handled locally without unwinding the stack.
  • Explicit: the caller sees a code and decides the next step.
  • Good for recoverable outcomes, like parsing user input.
  • Costs: cluttering checks and risk of ignored returns.
Concrete example
A divide function returns (status, result) where status 0 means success and negative values indicate specific input or runtime errors.
Code Example
def divide_numbers_with_code(numerator, denominator):
  if denominator == 0:
    return -1, "Error: Cannot divide by zero."
  if not isinstance(numerator, (int, float)) or not isinstance(denominator, (int, float)):
    return -2, "Error: Invalid input types."
  return 0, numerator / denominator

# Caller:
status, result = divide_numbers_with_code(10, 2)
if status == 0:
  print(f"Result: {result}")
else:
  print(f"Failed: {result}")
Key Takeaway

Choose error codes for common, expected failures and ensure callers consistently check returned status.

screens.title: What are Exceptions?
screens.narratorSegment: Exceptions are a language-level mechanism that interrupt normal execution by raising an object that carries context. When an exception is raised, the runtime unwinds the call stack until it finds a matching handler, or else the program ends with an error message and stack trace. Exceptions are well-suited for truly exceptional conditions that prevent the function from completing its contract, such as dividing by zero, a missing file, or a type mismatch. They separate error handling from the happy path, which keeps main logic clearer and forces handling at some level of the system. Exception objects convey rich context — messages, types, and stack traces — which makes diagnosing problems easier than many error codes. However, misuse is common: raising exceptions for routine control flow makes code harder to reason about and can degrade performance. Also, catching overly broad exceptions can mask bugs. Use specific exception types, include helpful messages, and only raise when callers cannot reasonably continue with normal operation. A concrete Python example shows TypeError for wrong inputs and ValueError for division by zero. Practice writing try-except blocks that catch these specific types and ensure that finally blocks or cleanup code still run as needed.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Exceptions interrupt flow to signal unexpected, unrecoverable, or exceptional conditions and carry contextual diagnostic information.

content.html:
Definition
Exceptions
Exceptions explained
Raise an exception when a function cannot fulfill its contract. Exceptions propagate until handled, enabling centralized error handling at the appropriate abstraction level.
  • Separate error code from normal logic.
  • Provide rich context: type, message, stack trace.
  • Use sparingly for unexpected or unrecoverable errors.
Code Example
def divide_numbers_with_exception(numerator, denominator):
  if not isinstance(numerator, (int, float)) or not isinstance(denominator, (int, float)):
    raise TypeError("Invalid input types. Both numerator and denominator must be numbers.")
  if denominator == 0:
    raise ValueError("Cannot divide by zero.")
  return numerator / denominator

# Caller:
try:
  result = divide_numbers_with_exception(10, 0)
except ValueError as e:
  print(f"Caught a ValueError: {e}")
except TypeError as e:
  print(f"Caught a TypeError: {e}")
finally:
  print("Division attempt complete.")
Key Takeaway

Raise and catch specific exception types so handlers can respond correctly and maintain diagnostic information.

screens.title: Pros and Cons: Error Codes vs Exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: When choosing between error codes and exceptions, weigh several practical trade-offs. Error codes are explicit and make error handling visible in the function signature or return value; they are useful when failure is a common, expected outcome. However, they clutter caller code with repetitive checks and are easy to forget — the most frequent problem is an unchecked status that silently allows incorrect program state. Exceptions keep the main path clean and force handling by propagating until a handler is found, which improves separation of concerns and provides richer debugging context. But exceptions can be misused: using them for normal control flow reduces clarity and performance, and catching broad exception types can hide bugs. Another dimension is context: exceptions carry stack traces and messages; error codes often require extra mechanisms to convey the same detail. Consider an A P I that searches for a user: returning None for a missing user signals an expected outcome, while raising an exception for an internal A P I failure signals something truly wrong. The right choice is contextual: prefer sentinel returns for routine results and exceptions for problems that callers must treat as errors. Always document the contract so callers know which behavior to expect.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off
keyIdea.text: Error codes fit expected failures and local handling; exceptions fit unexpected failures and centralized handling with richer diagnostics.

content.html:
Comparison
Error Codes — Pros & Cons
  • Pros: Explicit, predictable, suitable for frequent, recoverable failures.
  • Cons: Caller must check status, code clutter, limited context.
Incorrect usage often leads to silent failures when checks are omitted.
Exceptions — Pros & Cons
  • Pros: Keeps main flow clean, forces handling higher up, carries context via exception objects.
  • Cons: Misuse for normal flow is confusing; broad catches can hide bugs.
Good practice: catch specific exceptions and re-raise or log unexpected exceptions.
Concrete scenario
When a user lookup may legitimately return nothing, returning None is cleaner. When the external service fails with a server error, raise an ApiException so the caller knows the failure is exceptional and worth retrying or alerting ops.

screens.title: Deciding Between Return Values and Exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Designing failure behavior benefits from a small checklist you can apply consistently. First, ask: is this failure an expected outcome in normal operation? If yes, prefer a sentinel return like None, an empty collection, or an explicit (value, success_flag) tuple. Second, consider caller responsibility: will every caller realistically check a status? If not, an exception may be safer to avoid silent errors. Third, assess diagnostic needs: if you need stack traces and detailed context for debugging, exceptions are more informative. Fourth, think about performance and hot paths: exceptions are heavier when used frequently, so avoid them in tight loops for normal conditions. Finally, document the contract so callers know whether they should check returns or catch exceptions. Apply this process when designing a public A P I or refactoring legacy code; it helps you make consistent, testable choices. A common misconception is to treat all failures the same; instead, classify failures and apply the right mechanism for each class. The result is cleaner code and fewer surprises for callers. Deciding Between Return Values and Exceptions means classify failures as expected or exceptional, consider caller behavior and diagnostic needs, and document the api contract.. In practical terms, a short decision checklist you can apply in api design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Try-Except Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: A robust try-except pattern begins by catching the smallest set of exception types you can handle. Catching ValueError to handle conversion issues or FileNotFoundError for missing files gives you a clear recovery path and preserves other unexpected exceptions so they can surface. Inside an except block, add context: include filenames, parameters, or line numbers in the message or in a wrapped custom exception. If you cannot meaningfully handle the error, re-raise the same exception or raise a new, higher-level exception that preserves the original as the cause. Avoid empty except blocks or 'except Exception as e: pass' which hide problems and make debugging impossible. Use finally to run cleanup actions that must always occur. Also, avoid using exceptions for expected loop-level control. For example, when converting many strings to integers, handle conversion errors locally and continue, or validate inputs earlier. Use logging in exception handlers so operational teams can diagnose failures. A small code walkthrough demonstrates catching TypeError and ValueError explicitly, logging the details, and allowing unexpected exceptions to propagate up. That pattern yields safer, more maintainable code. Try-Except Best Practices means catch specific exceptions, add context, log or re-raise when appropriate, and never silently swallow errors.. In practical terms, catch specific exceptions, provide context, and avoid swallowing errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Pattern: specific excepts with context
def safe_divide(numerator, denominator):
  try:
    if not isinstance(numerator, (int, float)):
      raise TypeError("numerator must be a number")
    if not isinstance(denominator, (int, float)):
      raise TypeError("denominator must be a number")
    if denominator == 0:
      raise ValueError("denominator is zero")
    return numerator / denominator
  except (TypeError, ValueError) as e:
    # Provide context and re-raise or return a sentinel as appropriate
    raise
Guidelines & example
Log the exception with context, and if you cannot handle it at this level, re-raise. Use finally to close resources. Do not use generic 'except Exception' unless you log and re-raise.
Misconception: "Catching all exceptions makes code safer." In truth, it often hides bugs and leads to harder to diagnose failures. Prefer targeted handlers and clear logging.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Starter implementation (refined)
class InvalidFileDataError(Exception):
  def __init__(self, filepath, line_num, line_text):
    super().__init__(f"Invalid data in {filepath} at line {line_num}: '{line_text}'")
    self.filepath = filepath
    self.line_num = line_num
    self.line_text = line_text

def process_file_data(filepath):
  total_sum = 0
  try:
    with open(filepath, 'r') as f:
      for line_num, line in enumerate(f, 1):
        text = line.strip()
        try:
          value = int(text)
          total_sum += value
        except ValueError:
          # Treat non-integer lines as exceptional with context
          raise InvalidFileDataError(filepath, line_num, text)
    return total_sum
  except FileNotFoundError:
    raise
Caller example
try:
  total = process_file_data('test_data.txt')

screens.title: Swallowing Exceptions and Catching Generic Exception
screens.narratorSegment: Two of the most damaging patterns are swallowing exceptions and catching broad exception classes. Swallowing exceptions occurs when code catches an error and does nothing — a quiet 'pass' — which hides failures and allows the program to continue in an invalid state. The result is silent corruption that often surfaces far later and is hard to trace. Catching generic exceptions, for example using 'except Exception' for broad error handling, is equally risky: it masks different problems, conflates recoverable and unrecoverable conditions, and can swallow keyboard interrupts or system exceptions in some environments. Instead, inspect the code in the try block to determine the actual exception types that can occur and catch only those. When you must handle many types at once, log details and re-raise if you cannot resolve the underlying issue. A useful refactor pattern is to add logging and a comment about why a catch is broad, or to wrap an unexpected exception in a higher-level custom exception that preserves the original as the cause for diagnostics. In code review, flag empty except blocks and broad except Exception handlers for closer scrutiny. The safest approach is explicitness and informative logs.

keyIdea.title: Pitfall
keyIdea.text: Never silently swallow exceptions and avoid catching overly broad exception classes; always log, handle, or re-raise with context.

content.html:
Common Mistakes
Swallowing exceptions
Do not use empty except blocks. They hide errors and make debugging impossible.
# Dangerous
try:
  value = int(input_value)
except ValueError:
  pass  # silently ignores bad input
Better: log the issue, provide user feedback, or raise a clearer exception so the caller can decide.
Catching Exception broadly
Using 'except Exception' masks many root causes and conflates them with recoverable errors.
# Risky
try:
  do_work()
except Exception as e:
  handle_error()  # hides underlying error
Better: catch specific exceptions, log details, and re-raise if you cannot fully handle them.

screens.title: Exception Propagation and the Call Stack
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding how exceptions propagate through the call stack helps you choose where to handle errors. When an exception is raised, control leaves the current function and moves up the call chain searching for an except block that matches the exception type. If no handler is found, the program terminates and usually prints a stack trace. This propagation is powerful: it allows low-level code to report problems and let higher-level code decide recoverability. For instance, a low-level file parser can raise InvalidFileDataError and let a top-level application handler catch it to present a user-friendly message, retry, or abort. Avoid catching too low in the stack unless you can actually fix the issue; catching at the wrong level leads to ad-hoc workarounds and duplicated recovery logic. A misconception is thinking propagation is unpredictable — in fact, it's deterministic: an exception always moves upward until a match is found. Use that determinism to centralize logging, retries, or cleanup in a small number of well-documented handlers. When designing libraries, document which exceptions you raise so callers know what to expect and where to handle them.

content.html:
Propagation
Call stack example
A function deep in the stack raises ValueError. No local handler exists, so the error travels up to the caller, and so on, until a matching except ValueError is found.
main() ➜ calls process_file()
process_file() ➜ calls parse_line()
parse_line() ➜ raises InvalidFileDataError
Design implication: handle where you have enough context to decide whether to retry, log detailed diagnostics, or convert to a user-level message.
Practical tips
  • Document which exceptions your functions may raise.
  • Handle errors at the layer that can decide recovery or escalate.
  • Use centralized logging handlers to record stack traces for ops.

screens.title: Design Question: API Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Apply what you learned to a realistic assessment: a function fetch_user_data(user_id) that queries a remote A P I. If the A P I returns 404, the user simply doesn't exist — this is often an expected outcome. Returning None or an empty result is a clear, low-friction approach that lets callers test presence without dealing with exceptions. If the A P I returns 500, that indicates an internal server failure — an exceptional condition that should raise an ApiException or another specific exception so the caller can retry, escalate, or log an incident. Returning error codes for remote failures is less idiomatic in modern code and places the burden on every caller to inspect status values. The assessment in the chapter advocates returning None for 404 and raising for 500, because that cleanly distinguishes expected absence from server-side failures. When designing the client, document these behaviors and write unit tests that simulate both responses, verifying callers handle the None path and catch ApiException for server errors. That exercise trains you to map HTTP semantics to language-level failure mechanisms consistently. content.html:
Assessment Idea
Scenario
fetch_user_data hits an external API. 404 means the user is absent; 500 means server error.
# Recommended behavior
# 404 -> return None
# 500 -> raise ApiException
Why this mapping?
  • 404 is an expected outcome callers often check for.
  • 500 is exceptional and must be handled differently (retry/alert).

Map expected HTTP outcomes to sentinel returns and exceptional server problems to raised exceptions; document and unit-test the behavior.

screens.title: Refactoring Error Code Style to Exceptions
screens.narratorSegment: A small refactor illustrates the advantages of exceptions: start with a function that returns status codes and messages. Identify the failure modes and replace status returns with raises that use clear exception types and messages. For example, take the divide_numbers_with_code function and convert its negative status codes into TypeError for invalid inputs and ValueError for zero denominator. Update callers to use try-except and eliminate repetitive status checks scattered through the codebase. The refactor reduces noise, centralizes error handling, and adds stack traces that help diagnose where a problem originated. Still, before refactoring, confirm that failures were indeed exceptional and not part of normal control flow. If a failure is common and callers intentionally branch on it, keep or redesign the A P I to return a clearly documented sentinel. After refactoring, run unit tests to ensure behavior is equivalent for success cases and that handlers manage the raised exceptions as intended. This step-by-step change keeps behavior predictable while improving readability and debuggability. keyIdea.title: Refactor
keyIdea.text: Convert status-return functions into exception-raising ones when failures are exceptional; update callers to handle exceptions cleanly.

content.html:
Refactor Demo
Before: error codes
def divide_numbers_with_code(numerator, denominator):
  if denominator == 0:
    return -1, "Error: Cannot divide by zero."
  if not isinstance(numerator, (int, float)):
    return -2, "Error: Invalid input types."
  return 0, numerator / denominator
After: exceptions
def divide_numbers_with_exception(numerator, denominator):
  if not isinstance(numerator, (int, float)) or not isinstance(denominator, (int, float)):
    raise TypeError("Invalid input types. Both numerator and denominator must be numbers.")
  if denominator == 0:
    raise ValueError("Cannot divide by zero.")
  return numerator / denominator
Run tests to confirm callers still behave correctly. If callers expected status codes, update them to try-except patterns; this centralizes error handling and surfaces real problems faster.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three ideas in mind as you design or refactor error handling. First, error codes are explicit and useful when failures are expected and recoverable; they require disciplined checking by callers. Second, exceptions are appropriate for exceptional conditions; they carry rich diagnostic context and allow centralized handling, but they must be used sparingly and caught specifically. Third, avoid common pitfalls: never silently swallow exceptions, and avoid catching overly broad exception classes without logging or re-raising. When in doubt, ask whether the failure is part of normal operation or a surprising event. That decision determines whether to return a sentinel value or raise an exception. Document the contract, write tests that simulate both normal and exceptional responses, and ensure handlers include enough context to act or to report. These habits improve reliability, debuggability, and code clarity across your project.

In this lesson we map two common ways functions communicate failure: returning error codes and raising exceptions. You will understand their trade-offs, see concrete Python examples, and learn a practical rule: use exceptions for truly exceptional conditions and use sentinel returns or explicit result values for expected, recoverable outcomes. We'll ground theory with a small divide function and a file-processing exercise so you can practice raising and catching specific errors. As we progress, you’ll spot three common mistakes: using exceptions for normal control flow, swallowing exceptions without logging, and catching broad exception classes that hide problems. Each of these mistakes undermines reliability and slows debugging. By the end, you’ll be able to decide which approach fits a given A P I and how to structure try-except blocks that convey useful context. Think of error codes like traffic lights at many intersections — predictable and local — and exceptions like an ambulance that changes global flow when something truly wrong happens. Consider the functions you write: do callers expect failure as a normal outcome, or is failure surprising? That question will guide everything you see next.

These objectives guide practice and assessment. First, you will compare and contrast error codes and exceptions: that means not just naming them, but explaining how they change control flow, caller responsibilities, and debuggability. Second, you will decide when to use exceptions for truly exceptional conditions and when to return sentinel values for expected, recoverable outcomes; this helps you design clean APIs that communicate intent. Third, you will implement robust exception handling in Python using try-except blocks and specific exception types, including raising informative, contextual exceptions. Fourth, you will discuss common mistakes — such as using exceptions for routine control flow, catching overly broad exception classes, or swallowing errors — and apply best practices like logging, re-raising, and choosing the right abstraction level for handlers. Each objective includes a small practice milestone so you can verify competence: explain trade-offs, refactor a function, write a file-processing routine that raises a custom error, and critique a legacy try-except that hides issues. These are skills you’ll want to apply in code reviews and production systems to reduce bugs and improve clarity.

This second objectives screen turns each goal into a concrete milestone you can practice. For comparison, make a small test that calls a function using both error-code and exception styles and document how callers change. For decision-making, take three real A P I examples and mark which failures are expected and which are exceptional and justify your choice. For implementation, write try-except blocks that catch specific exceptions, include contextual messages, and re-raise when appropriate. For common mistakes, locate a legacy handler that uses broad exception catches or a silent pass and refactor it into specific handlers with logging and clear behavior. Each milestone teaches a different skill: diagnosis, judgement, coding practice, and code hygiene. Treat these as bite-sized lab tasks you can complete in code reviews or as unit tests. When you can demonstrate each milestone, you’ve not only learned the theory but shown practical, safety-conscious coding habits that improve maintainability and observability.

Error codes are explicit return values reserved to communicate success or specific failure types from a function. Historically they appear as integers or tuples where one part is a status and the other is the result or message. The defining characteristic is that the caller must inspect the returned status to detect failures. A straightforward advantage is predictability: when failure is common or expected, returning a sentinel value keeps control local and avoids unwinding the call stack. For example, a parse function may return None or a pair (value, success_flag) when parsing user input is routine and failing is not surprising. But that safety comes at a cost. Requiring the caller to always check the status clutters code and is easy to forget, producing silent failures. Error codes also tend to carry limited diagnostic context compared to exceptions. In practice, clean APIs use sentinel returns for expected, recoverable conditions — for instance, a lookup that might legitimately return no result — and reserve error codes with clear documentation, consistent values, and helper functions to unpack them. A common misconception is thinking error codes are inherently safer; they are explicit but place the burden on every caller. The takeaway: use error codes intentionally for normal, anticipated failures and structure callers to check and handle the codes.

Exceptions are a language-level mechanism that interrupt normal execution by raising an object that carries context. When an exception is raised, the runtime unwinds the call stack until it finds a matching handler, or else the program ends with an error message and stack trace. Exceptions are well-suited for truly exceptional conditions that prevent the function from completing its contract, such as dividing by zero, a missing file, or a type mismatch. They separate error handling from the happy path, which keeps main logic clearer and forces handling at some level of the system. Exception objects convey rich context — messages, types, and stack traces — which makes diagnosing problems easier than many error codes. However, misuse is common: raising exceptions for routine control flow makes code harder to reason about and can degrade performance. Also, catching overly broad exceptions can mask bugs. Use specific exception types, include helpful messages, and only raise when callers cannot reasonably continue with normal operation. A concrete Python example shows TypeError for wrong inputs and ValueError for division by zero. Practice writing try-except blocks that catch these specific types and ensure that finally blocks or cleanup code still run as needed.

When choosing between error codes and exceptions, weigh several practical trade-offs. Error codes are explicit and make error handling visible in the function signature or return value; they are useful when failure is a common, expected outcome. However, they clutter caller code with repetitive checks and are easy to forget — the most frequent problem is an unchecked status that silently allows incorrect program state. Exceptions keep the main path clean and force handling by propagating until a handler is found, which improves separation of concerns and provides richer debugging context. But exceptions can be misused: using them for normal control flow reduces clarity and performance, and catching broad exception types can hide bugs. Another dimension is context: exceptions carry stack traces and messages; error codes often require extra mechanisms to convey the same detail. Consider an A P I that searches for a user: returning None for a missing user signals an expected outcome, while raising an exception for an internal A P I failure signals something truly wrong. The right choice is contextual: prefer sentinel returns for routine results and exceptions for problems that callers must treat as errors. Always document the contract so callers know which behavior to expect.

Designing failure behavior benefits from a small checklist you can apply consistently. First, ask: is this failure an expected outcome in normal operation? If yes, prefer a sentinel return like None, an empty collection, or an explicit (value, success_flag) tuple. Second, consider caller responsibility: will every caller realistically check a status? If not, an exception may be safer to avoid silent errors. Third, assess diagnostic needs: if you need stack traces and detailed context for debugging, exceptions are more informative. Fourth, think about performance and hot paths: exceptions are heavier when used frequently, so avoid them in tight loops for normal conditions. Finally, document the contract so callers know whether they should check returns or catch exceptions. Apply this process when designing a public A P I or refactoring legacy code; it helps you make consistent, testable choices. A common misconception is to treat all failures the same; instead, classify failures and apply the right mechanism for each class. The result is cleaner code and fewer surprises for callers. Keep three ideas in mind as you design or refactor error handling. First, error codes are explicit and useful when failures are expected and recoverable; they require disciplined checking by callers. Second, exceptions are appropriate for exceptional conditions; they carry rich diagnostic context and allow centralized handling, but they must be used sparingly and caught specifically. Third, avoid common pitfalls: never silently swallow exceptions, and avoid catching overly broad exception classes without logging or re-raising. When in doubt, ask whether the failure is part of normal operation or a surprising event. That decision determines whether to return a sentinel value or raise an exception. Document the contract, write tests that simulate both normal and exceptional responses, and ensure handlers include enough context to act or to report. These habits improve reliability, debuggability, and code clarity across your project.

Use this quick reference when writing or reviewing code. First, classify failures: if a case is part of normal behavior, return a sentinel value or None; if it prevents a function from fulfilling its contract, raise an exception. Second, be explicit: catch concrete exception types, add context when raising, and avoid empty except blocks. Third, test and document: write unit tests for both expected absence paths and exceptional server or input and output failures, and document which exceptions a function may raise. These rules make code more predictable, easier to debug, and safer in production. Before you commit, ask: will a caller reasonably check a return status, or should this be an exception?
